claim: Neural circuits for behavior transform sensory inputs into motor outputs in patterns with strategic value.
source: Neural circuits for behavior transform sensory inputs into motor outputs in patterns with strategic value.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuits presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations.

claim: CsChrimson is a red-shifted variant of channelrhodopsin.
source: We express CsChrimson, a red-shifted variant of channelrhodopsin, in specific chemosensory neurons and expose large numbers of freely moving animals to random optogenetic activation patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CsChrimson, a known optogenetic tool.

claim: Linear-nonlinear models accurately predict navigational decision-making for different optogenetic activation waveforms in Drosophila larva.
source: We find that linear–nonlinear models accurately predict navigational decision-making for different optogenetic activation waveforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and related figures.

claim: Drosophila larva navigation involves regulation of transitions between runs and turns.
source: Drosophila larva navigation involves the regulation of transitions between two basic motor states, runs during which the animal moves forward using rhythmic peristaltic waves and turns during which the larva sweeps its head back and forth until it selects the direction of a new run (Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During runs, larvae move forward using rhythmic peristaltic waves.
source: Drosophila larva navigation involves the regulation of transitions between two basic motor states, runs during which the animal moves forward using rhythmic peristaltic waves and turns during which the larva sweeps its head back and forth until it selects the direction of a new run (Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During turns, larvae sweep their heads back and forth until selecting the direction of a new run.
source: Drosophila larva navigation involves the regulation of transitions between two basic motor states, runs during which the animal moves forward using rhythmic peristaltic waves and turns during which the larva sweeps its head back and forth until it selects the direction of a new run (Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Attractive and repulsive responses can be estimated by the tendency of larvae to aggregate near or avoid an environmental stimulus.
source: Attractive and repulsive responses can be estimated by the tendency of the larva to aggregate near or avoid an environmental stimulus (Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When larvae encounter improving conditions over time, they lower the likelihood of ending each run with a turn, thereby lengthening runs in favorable directions.
source: When the larva encounters improving conditions over time, it lowers the likelihood of ending each run with a turn, thereby lengthening runs in favorable directions.
evidence: This is a description of larval behavior based on established knowledge of chemotaxis.

claim: When larvae encounter improving conditions during head sweeps of a turn, they increase the likelihood of starting a new run, thereby starting more runs in favorable directions.
source: When the larva encounters improving conditions during each head sweep of a turn, it increases the likelihood of starting a new run, thereby starting more runs in favorable directions.
evidence: This is a description of larval behavior based on established knowledge of chemotaxis.

claim: Attractants tend to suppress transitions from runs to turns and stimulate transitions from turns to runs in larvae.
source: Thus, subjecting the larva to an attractant tends to suppress transitions from runs to turns and stimulate transitions from turns to runs; subjecting the larva to a repellant has the opposite effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral patterns described earlier in the text.

claim: Repellants have opposite effects to attractants on larval motor state transitions.
source: Thus, subjecting the larva to an attractant tends to suppress transitions from runs to turns and stimulate transitions from turns to runs; subjecting the larva to a repellant has the opposite effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral patterns described earlier in the text.

claim: CsChrimson is activated at wavelengths that are invisible to the larva's phototaxis system.
source: The recent development of a red-shifted version of channelrhodopsin, CsChrimson, which is activated at wavelengths that are invisible to the larva's phototaxis system, now allows us to specifically manipulate the activity of neurons in behaving animals with reliability and reproducibility (Klapoetke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the work describing CsChrimson.

claim: Optogenetic illumination at 1.9 W/m² and 625 nm reliably activates CsChrimson in Or45a-expressing ORNs.
source: We made extracellular recordings of the dorsal organ (DO) of individual larvae expressing CsChrimson in specific ORNs and recorded the responses to red light activation pulses of 0.2, 0.5, and 1 s of the same intensity used in the behavioral experiments. We found that optogenetic activation of the ORN-expressing Or45a reliably and reproducibly induced spike trains during exposure to red light (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Optogenetic illumination at 1.9 W/m² and 625 nm reliably activates CsChrimson in Or42a-expressing ORNs.
source: Similar results were obtained using larvae expressing CsChrimson in the ORN-expressing Or42a (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Orco-expressing neurons mediates an attractive response in larvae.
source: Random optogenetic activation of all the ORNs via expression of UAS-CsChrimson with the Orco olfactory-receptor-coreceptor driver (previously called Or83b) mediated an attractive response similar to the one shown with the Or42a driver alone (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Most ORNs in Drosophila larva are thought to mediate attractant responses.
source: This is consistent with most ORNs in the Drosophila larva being thought to mediate attractant responses (Kreher et al., 2008; Mathew et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Or45a-expressing ORN mediates an aversive response.
source: One exception is the Or45a-expressing ORN, which has recently been shown to mediate an aversive response in an optogenetic setup; larvae that express channelrhodopsin in Or45a-expressing neurons will avoid an illuminated region of an agar plate (Bellmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Or45a-expressing neurons are the only ORNs that detect octyl acetate.
source: A role for the Or45a-expressing neurons in repellency is also consistent with the observation that they are the only ORNs that detect octyl acetate, a chemical repellant (Cobb and Dannet, 1994; Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Octyl acetate is a chemical repellant for Drosophila larvae.
source: A role for the Or45a-expressing neurons in repellency is also consistent with the observation that they are the only ORNs that detect octyl acetate, a chemical repellant (Cobb and Dannet, 1994; Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Run-to-turn transitions in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination.
source: Run-to-turn transitions in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae coincided with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination and turn-to-run transitions coincided with a decrease, consistent with repellant behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Turn-to-run transitions in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with a decrease in the probability of optogenetic illumination.
source: Run-to-turn transitions in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae coincided with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination and turn-to-run transitions coincided with a decrease, consistent with repellant behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Runs decelerate approximately 1 second before the onset of head-sweeping behavior.
source: We measured the crawling speeds of larvae before flagged run-to-turn transitions and found that runs decelerate ∼1 s before the onset of head-sweeping behavior (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The average deceleration time was 1 second for all experiments conducted in this study.
source: The average deceleration time was 1 s for all experiments conducted in this study (Student's t-test, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Or42a receptor is activated by ethyl butyrate and ethyl acetate.
source: The Or42a receptor is activated by a number of volatile chemoattractants including ethyl butyrate and ethyl acetate (Louis et al., 2007; Kreher et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Genetically modified animals in which Or42a-expressing ORN is the only functional ORN are capable of climbing olfactory gradients towards attractants.
source: Genetically modified animals in which the Or42a-expressing ORN is the only functional ORN are capable of climbing olfactory gradients towards these attractants.
evidence: This is stated as an observation, likely from previous studies or established knowledge.

claim: Or42a-expressing ORN mediates attractant responses.
source: These observations strongly suggest that the Or42a-expressing ORN mediates attractant responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral observations described.

claim: Run-to-turn transitions in Or42a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with a decrease in the probability of optogenetic activation.
source: We found that run-to-turn transitions coincided with a decrease in the probability of optogenetic activation (Figure 2A, left), whereas turn-to-run transitions coincided with an increase (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Turn-to-run transitions in Or42a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with an increase in the probability of optogenetic activation.
source: We found that run-to-turn transitions coincided with a decrease in the probability of optogenetic activation (Figure 2A, left), whereas turn-to-run transitions coincided with an increase (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The static nonlinearity for run-to-turn transition in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae is fitted using a sigmoidal function with R² = 0.8792.
source: The static nonlinearity for the run-to-turn transition is fitted using least squares estimation of a sigmoidal function (R2 = 0.8792).
evidence: This is supported by the fitting analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The static nonlinearity for turn-to-run transition in Or45a>CsChrimson larvae is fitted with a line with R² = 0.5041.
source: The static nonlinearity for the turn-to-run transition is fitted with a line (R2 = 0.5041).
evidence: This is supported by the fitting analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LN model predictions show remarkably good agreement with experimental measurements for step increases in optogenetic illumination and defined trains of pulses.
source: We found remarkably good agreement in these predictions to both stimulus types (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of predictions and experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The LN prediction begins to fail to account for turn-to-run transitions at long times following a step increase in optogenetic illumination.
source: We note that the LN prediction begins to fail to account for the turn-to-run transitions at long times following a step increase in optogenetic illumination.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Turns typically last less than 4 seconds.
source: Turns typically last <4 s, which limits the length of stimulus history that can be used in a linear filter, which thus puts a ∼4-s upper bound on the length of stimulus response that can be predicted.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of larval behavior.

claim: Gr21a receptor senses carbon dioxide.
source: The Gr21a receptor senses carbon dioxide, a powerful Drosophila repellant (Faucher et al., 2006; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Carbon dioxide is a powerful Drosophila repellant.
source: The Gr21a receptor senses carbon dioxide, a powerful Drosophila repellant (Faucher et al., 2006; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Run-to-turn transitions in Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination from baseline.
source: We found that run-to-turn transitions coincided with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination from baseline, whereas turn-to-run transitions coincided with a decrease (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Turn-to-run transitions in Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with a decrease in the probability of optogenetic illumination.
source: We found that run-to-turn transitions coincided with an increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination from baseline, whereas turn-to-run transitions coincided with a decrease (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The linear filter for Gr21a run-to-turn transition has a pronounced negative lobe lasting approximately 1.5 seconds preceding the positive lobe.
source: This positive lobe was itself preceded by a pronounced negative lobe lasting ∼1.5 s for Gr21a but not for Or45a.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the event-triggered stimulus histories shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Biphasic linear filters contribute to adaptation following transient stimulation.
source: Biphasic linear filters—such as that associated with Gr21a and also seen in other sensory systems like the Escherichia coli chemotactic response—contribute to adaptation following transient stimulation (Block et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on E. coli chemotaxis.

claim: The probability of run-to-turn transition returns to baseline faster for Gr21a than Or45a following a step increase in repellant stimulation.
source: The probability of run-to-turn transition returns to baseline faster in the case of Gr21a.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and predictions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: P(r→t) of Gr21a larvae reach values significantly higher than baseline at least 0.5 seconds earlier than Or45a larvae.
source: We found that P(r → t) of Gr21a larvae reach values significantly higher than baseline at least 0.5 s earlier than Or45a larvae.
evidence: This is supported by z-test analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Or45a larvae stay at elevated values of P(r→t) for at least 0.75 seconds longer than Gr21a larvae.
source: In addition, Or45a larvae stay at elevated values of P(r → t) for at least 0.75 s longer than Gr21a larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by z-test analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Gr2a is expressed in the A1 and A2 GRNs of the dorsal organ and in two unidentified neurons in the terminal organ.
source: Gr2a is expressed in the A1 and A2 GRNs of the DO as well as in two unidentified neurons in the terminal organ (Kwon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Gr2a is part of the subfamily of Gr68a, which has been identified as a pheromone receptor in the adult fly.
source: The role of the Gr2a receptor is not known, but it is part of the subfamily of Gr68a, which has been identified as a pheromone receptor in the adult fly (Bray and Amrein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Run-to-turn transitions in Gr2a>CsChrimson larvae coincide with a decrease in optogenetic activation.
source: We calculated the event-triggered stimulus histories of Gr2a>CsChrimson larvae and found that run-to-turn transitions coincided with a decrease in optogenetic activation, consistent with an attractant response (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Or42a larvae reach different steady states of P(r→t) for lights ON versus lights OFF.
source: The most noticeable feature is that Or42a larvae reach different steady states of P(r → t) for lights ON or OFF; this creates differences in step-response dynamics.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Or42a larvae take at least 1.75 seconds longer than Gr2a larvae for P(r→t) to become significantly higher than the lights OFF steady-state P(r→t).
source: Because Or42a larvae start at a lower P(r → t), they take at least 1.75 s longer than Gr2a larvae for P(r → t) to become significantly higher than the lights OFF steady-state P(r → t).
evidence: This is supported by z-test analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Linear filters for turn-to-run transitions show similar shape for all Gal4 drivers used in this study.
source: We note that unlike the linear filters for run-to-turn transitions, the linear filters for turn-to-run transitions showed a similar shape for all Gal4 drivers that we used in this study. These filters only showed some variation in amplitude (Figures 1, 2, 4, 5).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data across multiple figures.

claim: The Drosophila larva dorsal organ contains 21 ORNs that together express 25 members of the Or family of odorant receptors and the Orco coreceptor.
source: The 21 ORNs contained in the larval DO together express 25 members of the Or family of odorant receptors and the Orco coreceptor (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 10 GRNs distributed in the dorsal organ and terminal organ together express 28 members of the Gr family of gustatory receptors.
source: In contrast, 10 GRNs distributed in the DO and terminal organ—named A1, A2, B1, B2, and C1-C6—together express 28 members of the Gr family of gustatory receptors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the larval chemosensory system.

claim: Most ORNs express a single Or, while GRNs can express multiple Grs and each Gr can be expressed in multiple GRNs.
source: Whereas most ORNs express a single Or, GRNs can express multiple Grs and each Gr can be expressed in multiple GRNs (Kwon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The C1 neuron expresses 17 receptors.
source: The C1 neuron expresses 17 receptors, some of which are found in other neurons (e.g., Gr32a, which is also found in B2) and some of which are specific to C1 (e.g., Gr9a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GRN receptor expression.

claim: Most Grs are thought to respond to repulsive bitter compounds because they express the bitter markers Gr33a and Gr66a.
source: Most Grs are thought to respond to repulsive bitter compounds because they express the bitter markers Gr33a and Gr66a (Kwon et al., 2011), suggesting that C1 is a broadly tuned mediator of repellant responses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: C1 is a broadly tuned mediator of repellant responses.
source: Most Grs are thought to respond to repulsive bitter compounds because they express the bitter markers Gr33a and Gr66a (Kwon et al., 2011), suggesting that C1 is a broadly tuned mediator of repellant responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the receptor expression pattern and previous knowledge.

claim: Optogenetic activation of C1 using Gr9a>CsChrimson larvae evokes a weak repellant response.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, optogenetic activation of C1 with random stimuli using Gr9a>CsChrimson larvae evoked a weak repellant response where the run-to-turn transition coincided with a slight increase in the probability of optogenetic illumination (Figure 5A) (this response was significantly different than the control with p < 0.05, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and statistical analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of C1 together with B2 using Gr32a>CsChrimson larvae evokes a much stronger repellant response than C1 alone.
source: Optogenetic activation of C1 together with B2 using Gr32a>CsChrimson larvae evoked a much stronger repellant response (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of specifically the B2 neuron using Gr10>CsChrimson larvae evokes a repellant response.
source: Optogenetic activation of specifically the B2 neuron using Gr10>CsChrimson larvae evoked a repellant response (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of C1 together with C4 using Gr39a.b>CsChrimson larvae generates a strong repellant response.
source: Optogenetic activation of C1 together with C4 using Gr39a.b>CsChrimson larvae generated a strong repellant response (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the C2 neuron alone using Gr94a>CsChrimson larvae evokes a weak attractive response.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of the C2 neuron alone using Gr94a>CsChrimson larvae evoked a weak attractive response (Figure 5E) (this response was significantly different than the control with p < 0.05, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and statistical analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The C2 neuron expresses the bitter receptors Gr33a and Gr66a.
source: This is surprising because the C2 neuron also expresses the bitter receptors Gr33a and Gr66a, which should drive repellant responses, although these receptors are also found in other neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about receptor expression.

claim: Co-activation of C1 and C2 using Gr39a.a>CsChrimson larvae exhibits a much stronger repellant response than activation of C1 alone.
source: This hypothesis is supported by our observation that co-activation of C1 and C2 using Gr39a.a>CsChrimson larvae exhibited a much stronger repellant response than activation of C1 alone (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Co-activation of C1, C2, and C4 using Gr59d>CsChrimson larvae exhibits a strong repellant response.
source: Co-activation of C1, C2, and C4 using Gr59d>CsChrimson larvae also exhibited a strong repellant response (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The strongest repellant response was observed by co-activating C1-C4, B1, and B2 using Gr66a>CsChrimson larvae.
source: The strongest repellant response was observed by co-activating C1-C4, B1, and B2 using Gr66a>CsChrimson larvae (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: All larvae were raised in the dark at 22°C and fed yeast with 0.5 mM all-trans-retinal.
source: All larvae were raised in the dark at 22°C and fed yeast with 0.5 mM all-trans-retinal.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Late second-instar larvae were used for behavioral assays.
source: Larvae were thoroughly washed in water, and late second-instar larvae were selected under a dissecting microscope.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Groups of 20-30 larvae were placed in the center of agar plates and allowed to freely move for 20 minutes.
source: For spatial navigation assays, groups of 20–30 larvae were placed in the center of a ∼5-mm thick 22 × 22 cm agar (Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA) plate and allowed to freely move for 20 min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Animals were recorded with a CCD camera at 4 Hz.
source: Animals were recorded with a CCD Mightex camera with a long-pass (740 nm) infrared filter at 4 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Light stimulation was produced with a custom built LED matrix at 625 nm wavelength.
source: Light stimulation was produced with a custom built LED matrix assembled with SMD 5050 flexible LED strip lights of 12 V DC and 625 nm wavelength (LEDlightninghut.com) and controlled with an H-bridge driver and custom code written for a LabJack U3 controller.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Illumination uniformity was verified at 1.9 W/m² ± 0.06.
source: We verified uniform light intensity at 1.9 W/m2 ± 0.06.
evidence: This is a description of experimental verification.

claim: A Bernoulli process was used to produce the random stimulus.
source: To produce the random stimulus, a Bernoulli process was used. This process is wide-sense stationary, produces independent binary values (Lights ON or OFF) at every instant, and its autocorrelation function is the Dirac delta function.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: During illumination, 100% of OK6-Gal4>CsChrimson larvae stopped crawling.
source: Consistent with that, during illumination 100% of the 85 larvae tested stopped crawling during illumination and slowly recovered motility afterwards.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-activation of narrowly tuned GRNs that express fewer Grs may potentiate the repellant response of the broadly tuned C1 GRN.
source: One possibility is that co-activation of narrowly tuned GRNs that express fewer Grs potentiates the repellant response of the broadly tuned C1 GRN; however, this interpretation should be taken with caution since different Gal4 drivers may induce different spiking rates upon optogenetic activation with CsChrimson.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The attractant response driven by C2 may be inverted when additional gustatory neurons are recruited.
source: One possibility is that the attractant response driven by C2 is inverted when additional gustatory neurons are recruited.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.
